name: Treaty with the Umpqua-Cow Creek Band, 1853
nations: Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians
promises: Article 1: the band ceded its lands in the Umpqua Valley of south-western Oregon.
Article 2: a tract on Cow Creek was to be an Indian reserve until the President selected a permanent home for the band, with buildings and improvements there of equal value.
Article 3: $12,000 in all: $1,000 in goods by October 1, 1854 and $11,000 in twenty yearly instalments of $550 in blankets, clothing, provisions, stock or farm tools.
Article 4: two dwelling-houses and a five-acre field fenced, ploughed and seeded, at United States expense.

breaches.what: The Cow Creek Band says it never received the $12,000 the treaty promised, about 2.3 cents an acre when settlers paid the government $1.25 an acre, and never received the reservation the treaty promised.

landTaken: More than 800 square miles of south-western Oregon, as the band states (Cow Creek tribal history).
compensation: The treaty promised $12,000; the band says it was not received. A $1.5 million settlement was reached in 1984, according to the band.
today: The Western Oregon Indian Termination Act of August 13, 1954 (68 Stat. 724) named the Cow Creek among the tribes whose federal supervision and services were to end; it does not mention this treaty. Congress restored federal recognition on December 29, 1982 (Public Law 97-391), restoring rights under any federal treaty 'which may have been diminished or lost' under the 1954 Act. The band says it is buying back land in its homeland.

nationVoice.nation: Cow Creek Band of Umpqua Tribe of Indians
nationVoice.summary: Says it became landless under the treaty, never received the promised reservation or payment, was ignored for nearly a century and then terminated, and won back recognition in 1982.

plain.promised: $12,000 in goods and yearly instalments, a reserve on Cow Creek until a permanent home was chosen, and two houses and a fenced, ploughed field, in exchange for the band's Umpqua Valley lands.
plain.happened: The Cow Creek Band says it never received the $12,000 or the promised reservation. No formal finding of breach has been located.
plain.today: The band reports a $1.5 million settlement in 1984, which it holds as an endowment. Listed for termination in 1954, it regained federal recognition in 1982 and says it is buying back land.

openQuestions: No court or Claims Commission finding on the 1853 payment or the never-selected reservation was found; the 1984 Court of Claims settlement record itself was not opened, and its amount comes from the band.

The Rogue River Tribe v. United States litigation in the Court of Claims (No. 45231, 1946 and 1950) also named the Cow Creek band; its outcome could not be read because the opinion is behind a paywall.

Audit 2026-11-08: removed the 1954 Termination Act as a breach and changed the status from broken to contested. Rule 9 needs an Act that took or overrode what this treaty secured; the Act does not name the treaty, the band never received the reservation the treaty promised, so termination took no treaty land, and the 1982 Act restores treaty rights only in general words. The removed text also said Congress acted without the band's consent, which no source opened states. A finding that the $12,000 or the Cow Creek reserve was never provided would make this broken.
